marks.name: title
marks.text: Hi everyone, and welcome to today's mini-talk.

marks.name: lede
marks.text: In the next few minutes I want to demystify one of computing's most useful little tools: the hash function.

marks.name: definition-heading
marks.text: So let's start with the core idea.

marks.name: definition-body
marks.text: A hash function takes any input a word, a file, an entire movie and turns it into a fixed size fingerprint.

marks.name: diagram
marks.text: Take a look at the diagram. No matter what goes in on the left, the output is always the same length.

marks.name: property-deterministic
marks.text: Now, two properties to remember. First: the function is deterministic. The same input always produces the same output, every single time.

marks.name: property-avalanche
marks.text: Second: change one tiny bit of the input, and the entire output changes in a wild and unpredictable way. We call this the avalanche effect.

marks.name: uses-heading
marks.text: Okay, but why do we care? Here are three places you've already used hashes today, probably without realizing it.

marks.name: use-passwords
marks.text: Passwords. When you log into a site, the site doesn't store your password. It stores a hash of it. That way, even if the database leaks, your password stays secret.

marks.name: use-integrity
marks.text: File integrity. Ever downloaded a big file with a checksum next to it? That checksum is a hash. If your downloaded file's hash matches, you know it wasn't corrupted in transit.

marks.name: use-blockchain
marks.text: And of course, blockchains. Every block is named by its hash, and each block contains the hash of the previous one. That's literally the chain in "blockchain."

marks.name: closing
marks.text: That's the whole idea. A small, deterministic, ultra-sensitive fingerprint for any piece of data. Thanks for listening!
